                                  BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                  COMMENTS OF GOOGLE LLC

          Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (“Commission”),1 Google LLC (“Google”) submits these comments on

the Midcontinent Independent System Operator Inc.’s (“MISO”) Zero Injection Generator

Interconnection Agreement (“ZGIA”) proposal. The ZGIA proposal is a step forward. Google

applauds MISO for working constructively with stakeholders to develop the proposal, which will

help facilitate the timely and efficient interconnection of badly needed new generation capacity .

          Google has consistently supported efforts to accelerate the pace at which new generation

facilities are interconnected to the transmission system. Those efforts are particularly important

now given the rapid load growth experienced throughout much of the country, including in MISO.

The best way to ensure the reliability and affordability of our electricity system under those

conditions is to enable the development of more generation capacity .

          That goal—the development of new capacity—is as much an infrastructure problem as it

is anything else.2 Aging, over-burdened transmission facilities are the primary barrier to supply

to keeping pace with demand.          Accordingly, building out the nation’s power grid with new




    1
        18 C.F.R. § 385.211 (2026).
    2
     Interconnection of Large Loads to the Transmission System, Comments of Google LLC, Docket No. RM26-4-
000, at 2-3 (filed Nov. 21, 2025).
 transmission facilities and advanced transmission technologies is one of the most critical steps we

can take to ensure the reliability and affordability of the nation’s electricity system.

            Google also recognizes that building new energy infrastructure, especially electric

transmission, takes an exceedingly long time. And while Google supports efforts to accelerate

those processes, time is not a luxury that the electricity sector has. For that reason, Google has

also strongly supported “reforms that will expedite the interconnection of facilities that maximize

the use of existing infrastructure and minimize strain on the grid.”3 Locating electric generating

facilities close to the loads they will serve is one of the most efficient means of doing so . As a

matter of engineering, economics, and basic physics, generation sited near the load it serves puts

less strain on the grid and requires less investment in new or upgraded transmission infrastructure.

Solutions that capitalize on that fact by facilitating efforts to site generation near paired load

therefore minimize the network upgrades needed to interconnect new resources and, in turn,

accelerate the pace at which new generation comes online.

           The ZGIA proposal is a step in that direction. It recognizes the importance of accounting

for how a generator will operate in practice when studying generator interconnection requests,

including the reality that generators serving electrically proximate loads can “minimize the impact

on the transmission system.” 4 Specifically, the ZGIA would create a “study process tailored to the

operational characteristics of generation serving co-located load, including a study process that




    3
        Id. at 5-6.
    4
       Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., Zero Injection Generator Interconnection Agreement, Docket No.
ER26-3552-000, at 13-14 (filed Aug. 18, 2026) (“Transmittal”); see also Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 195
FERC ¶ 61,212, at P 113 (2026) (“Large Load Show Cause Order”) (“Where a generating facility’s output is matched
to the demand of the electrically proximate large load or large co-located load or if the generating facility’s output is
limited to ensure no new injection, the impacts to the transmission system of intercon necting the generating facility to
serve that electrically proximate large load or large co-located load may be limited, thereby potentially reducing the
need for Network Upgrades, which can accelerate the generator interconnection process.” (footnote omitted)).

                                                               -2-
 recognizes the potentially reduced Transmission System impacts where generation is limited to

serving its associated load.” 5 That is a major advancement beyond how transmission providers

typically study requests to interconnect to the grid—i.e., based on the assumption the generator

must be able to deliver its full output to the grid at all times—and crucial to adding as much

capacity to the existing transmission system as quickly as possible. On the latter point, MISO

suggests “the ZGIA process can take place quickly, with the ZG Impact Assessment completed

within 90 Calendar Days,”6 much faster than the multi-year timelines that can apply to generator

interconnection applications.

             The ZGIA is, however, only a step in the right direction. That is because the ZG

Interconnection Service can be used only to serve designated load that is either at the same Point

of Interconnection as the paired generator or has a Point of Withdrawal on the same voltage side

of the same substation as the paired generator.7 That limitation is considerably more restrictive in

practice than the reforms that the Commission proposed to require MISO to adopt in the Large

Load Show Cause Order.8 In that proceeding, the Commission described electrically proximate

load and generation as those that are no more than two substations apart.9 Similarly, SPP’s High

Impact Large Load Generation Assessment (“HILLGA”) process, which offers an expedited 90-

day interconnection study and a limited, provisional form of transmission service, is also available

to generators that are located within two substations of the large load they will serve.10

                                                         -3-
         As MISO develops its response to the directives in the Large Load Show Cause Order,

Google urges it to expand the principles established in the ZGIA to apply to circumstances at least

as broad as the within-two-substations configuration contemplated in the Large Load Show Cause

Order and permitted under HILLGA.           By including more potential load and generation

configurations, MISO can unlock more new generation on an expedited basis. That is particularly

so because the distinction between being at the same point of interconnection and within two

substations is a meaningful difference in practice. For example, a major energy park that includes

significant networked load and generation is exactly the type of facility for which a ZGIA

framework would make sense. But if, as is common in these configurations, that energy park has

multiple substations with the generation and associated load interconnecting through different

substations, the ZGIA avenue may be unavailable, leading to costly dela ys and unnecessary

expense in bringing the new generation online.

        At the same time, although Google urges MISO to make the most out of approaches like

ZGIA, MISO cannot lose sight of the importance of accelerating its principal interconnection

process: the Definitive Planning Process (“DPP”). As noted, it can take several years to move an

interconnection request through the DPP process.11 That timeline creates an understandable urge

to pursue short-term solutions to accelerate the interconnection of a limited subset of generator—

most notably, the Expedited Resource Addition Study (“ERAS”). Nevertheless, Google believes

that fixing the sluggish timelines in the DPP is a more durable and lasting solution to MISO

interconnection challenges than an endless series of shortcuts, even if some of those shortcuts are

merited for the foreseeable future.




   11
        MISO, Interconnection Process Working Group, DPP Study Schedule Updates (July 21, 2026),
https://cdn.misoenergy.org/20260721%20IPWG%20Item%2003b%20DPP%20Study%20Schedule769072.pdf .

                                                   -4-
          MISO appears to agree. In its ERAS filing, MISO stated that it “remains committed to

reducing its general interconnection review period to one year,” with a goal of doing so by 2028.12

This proceeding provides one window into how it might achieve that goal. Drawing on the idea

underpinning the ZGIA, MISO should amend the DPP study process to ensure that it is studying

generators as they actually intend to operate and based on the effects they can realistically be

expected to have on the system, which will avoid saddling generators with unnecessary network

upgrades that are required only to manage extreme circumstances. At the end of the day, MISO

needs a single, well-functioning generator interconnection process that can facilitate the timely

entry of new resources onto the system. Otherwise, the region’s supply of generation will

perpetually lag behind future increases in demand.

         In addition, Google strongly supports continued efforts to integrate transmission planning

and generator interconnection. MISO’s MTEP has been one of the country’s leading examples of

forward-looking transmission planning, particularly its Long-Range Transmission Plan. Holistic

transmission planning, that considers generator interconnection needs, among other drivers, helps

avoid the piece-meal, inefficient development of the transmission system while simultaneously

reducing the risk that interconnection customers will be forced to shoulder enormous network

upgrade costs that can stymie the development of new generation facilities and create considerable

uncertainty for other generators through restudies. “No power plant can obtain financing when the

transmission costs are either unknown or subject to significant revision based on ‘that next




    12
      Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., Revisions to the Open Access Transmission, Energy and Operating
Reserve Tariff Expedited Resource Addition Study Filing, Docket No. ER25 -2454-000, at 7 (filed June 6, 2025).

                                                         -5-
 study.’”13 The end result of which is a further delay in developing badly needed generation

capacity.

          This type of proactive transmission planning is also important for policy priorities like the

Ratepayer Protection Pledge, to which Google is a signatory, 14 as well as broader efforts to

incentivize customers to bring their own new capacity. Those policies and efforts, which are

consistent with Google’s longstanding energy procurement philosophy and essential to ensuring

reliable service and affordable rates for residential customers and other existing commercial

customers, simply will not succeed if new generation cannot get through the interconnection

queue. By expediting the interconnection of electrically proximate load and generation, ZGIA is

a step forward in that regard. But it is just a step. Many more are needed to win the race.



          Respectfully submitted,
